solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: American kills leader abandoning upper-class people (4)

indicatorNotes.leader abandoning: the leading letter walks away from the word, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: TOFFS without its first letter T

annotation.surface: A grim report of an American killer turning on the elite.
annotation.walkthrough: In American slang to off someone is to kill them. A toff is British slang for an upper-class person.
annotation.definitionFit: OFFS is the American slang verb 'kills', as in 'he offs the witness'.

entries.clue: Gear in Providence right in order for marine flyer (7,4)

annotation.surface: Someone trusts Providence to put a ship's equipment right before a sailor sets out.
annotation.walkthrough: The same small word 'in' does two separate insertions, one in each half. 'Order' is a command here, not tidiness, and 'Providence' is fate rather than the American city.
annotation.definitionFit: The frigatebird is a large tropical seabird, so it is a marine flyer.

entries.clue: Incidental illustration second one to please greatly (9)

annotation.surface: An editor praises a second picture in a book for charming the reader.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second one' reads like a phrase but splits into two single letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A sidelight is a piece of incidental information that illustrates a subject.

entries.clue: Insect infesting rubbish endlessly fed to dog (10)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: the word loses its end, its last letter
indicatorNotes.fed to: the letters are put inside the dog like food

blocks.note: a cocker spaniel, a breed of dog

annotation.surface: An insect has got into the scraps being given to a dog.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition runs on into 'infesting', so 'rubbish' seems to be what the insect infests; it belongs to the wordplay instead. Cockchafers are beetles that damage crops.
annotation.definitionFit: The cockchafer is a large European beetle whose grubs attack crop roots, an insect that infests fields.

entries.clue: Tundra dwellers you found beneath a ridge in county (7)

indicatorNotes.found beneath: in a down entry, beneath means placed after

blocks.note: a rib is a raised ridge
U = you, as in text speak

annotation.surface: A description of where you live, below a ridge in some county.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beneath' only works because this is a down entry, where one piece can sit under another.
annotation.definitionFit: Caribou are the reindeer of the northern tundra, and the plural caribou matches 'dwellers'.

entries.clue: US race trouble starts suddenly in city there? (8,7)

blocks.note: colour = race, in the American spelling

annotation.surface: A news story about racial trouble flaring up suddenly in an American city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'US' asks for the American spelling COLOR, without the U. 'There' points back to the US, so the definition is a city in America.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by location: 'there' points back to 'US', and Colorado Springs is a city in the American Rockies.

entries.clue: Relatively common boy necking a sherry regularly (7)

indicatorNotes.necking: to neck is to swallow, so the boy's word takes A inside it
indicatorNotes.regularly: things done regularly happen at even intervals, so letters are taken at even steps through the word

blocks.note: S, E and R, every other letter of SHERRY

annotation.surface: A lad knocking back a sherry now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boy' is not a lad but the exclamation 'Boy!', which is 'Cor!' in British speech.
annotation.definitionFit: Coarser means more common or vulgar, the comparative 'relatively' matching the -er ending.

entries.clue: Write up extract from manuscript (5)

indicatorNotes.Write up: in a down entry, writing upwards turns the letters round

blocks.note: an extract is an 'oil of' something, as in oil of cloves

annotation.surface: An instruction to make notes on a passage from an old manuscript.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extract from' reads as 'a passage taken from', but it is the phrase OIL OF, as in oil of cloves.
annotation.definitionFit: A folio is a leaf of a manuscript, or a manuscript volume made of such leaves.

entries.clue: What poets often do that Keats and Yeats don’t? (5)

annotation.definition: What poets often do that Keats and Yeats don’t?

blocks.note: the straight reading: poets usually make their lines chime
the twist: the two names look alike on paper but are said differently, so they fail to chime

annotation.surface: A question about the habits of poets.
annotation.walkthrough: Keats and Yeats look as if they should rhyme on paper, but they are said 'keets' and 'yates', so the two poets' names do not rhyme.
annotation.definitionFit: Poets often rhyme, and the names Keats and Yeats famously fail to.

entries.clue: Ancient folk tale incorrectly recalled in parts (10)

indicatorNotes.incorrectly: the letters are set down wrongly, out of order
indicatorNotes.parts: the word pushes two letters apart and sits between them

blocks.note: the word itself, placed between C and DERELLA

annotation.surface: Someone remembers an old fairy story wrongly, in bits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In parts' looks like 'in pieces', but IN is a piece of the answer and 'parts' tells it to split the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: Cinderella is a folk tale with versions going back to ancient Greece.

entries.clue: Savagely attack Frost’s first narrative poem (4)

indicatorNotes.first: Frost's first is the thing Frost starts with, his opening letter

blocks.note: a lay is a narrative poem or ballad

annotation.surface: A critic savaging Robert Frost's first narrative poem.
annotation.walkthrough: Frost suggests the American poet, which fits the poem, but only his initial is used.
annotation.definitionFit: To flay someone is to criticise them savagely, literally to strip off their skin.

entries.clue: Always interrupting fluent movement (3,3)

indicatorNotes.interrupting: one word breaks into the middle of the other

blocks.note: ay (or aye) = always, an old word

annotation.surface: Someone forever cutting into a graceful motion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Movement' seems to follow on from 'fluent' as a smooth motion; it is a political movement.
annotation.definitionFit: Gay Lib, short for gay liberation, was the campaign for gay rights, a movement.

entries.clue: Most here ailing? (4,4)

indicatorNotes.ailing: the letters are unwell, so they come out in a different state

annotation.surface: A question: are most of the people here unwell?
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: in a rest home most residents are indeed ailing.
annotation.definitionFit: A rest home cares for elderly or sick people, so most there may well be ailing.

entries.clue: Mother initially cradled him, ruined in Eliot’s work (11)

indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the start, so only the word's opening letter is used
indicatorNotes.ruined: the letters are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order

annotation.surface: A mother held her baby, and he was spoiled, all in a novel by Eliot.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface borrows the domestic drama of a Victorian novel. George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans.
annotation.definitionFit: Middlemarch is George Eliot's best-known novel.

entries.clue: He composed letter after a bit of work (4)

blocks.note: B is the letter that follows A in the alphabet
the erg is a small unit of work in physics

annotation.surface: A composer wrote a letter once he had done some work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Letter after' seems to mean a letter placed after something; the phrase to read is 'letter after a', which is B.
annotation.definitionFit: Alban Berg was an Austrian composer, so he composed.

entries.clue: Worry defender in America doesn’t give enough? (10)

indicatorNotes.Worry: to worry something is to shake it about, as a dog worries a bone

annotation.surface: A question about whether an American defender who gives too little should cause concern.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Worry' looks like a verb about fretting; it means shake up the letters of 'defender'.
annotation.definitionFit: To underfeed is to give too little food, so someone who underfeeds doesn't give enough.

entries.clue: Old bore’s spoken for well-known brand (9)

indicatorNotes.spoken: say the word and write what you hear

blocks.note: calibre = bore of a gun; said aloud it gives CALIBUR

annotation.surface: A dull old person has been booked to speak for a famous company.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brand' is an old word for a sword, and Excalibur is King Arthur's famous one. 'Bore' is a gun's calibre, not a dull person.
annotation.definitionFit: Excalibur is the most famous sword of legend, and brand is a poetic word for sword.

entries.clue: Police officer under pressure made to look worn (10)

annotation.surface: An overworked police officer starts to look worn out.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tired officer, but the definition is the furniture and fashion sense, as in distressed jeans.
annotation.definitionFit: Distressed wood or denim has been deliberately made to look worn.

entries.clue: Lured in — temperature cool in butt (7)

blocks.note: butt = end, as of a cigarette

annotation.surface: Someone tempted into a cold cellar where a barrel keeps things cool.
annotation.walkthrough: A butt is also a cask, but here it is the end of something, as in a cigarette butt.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to entice is to tempt someone into a place or act with bait or promises.

entries.clue: Hero elevated in Scotland knows devil (7)

indicatorNotes.elevated: in a down entry, raising the word turns it upside down
indicatorNotes.in Scotland: the word is the Scots one

annotation.surface: A Scots saying: a hero who is raised up knows the devil.
annotation.walkthrough: Dickens here is the old euphemism for the devil, as in 'what the dickens?', not the novelist.
annotation.definitionFit: 'The dickens' is a mild word for the devil, as in 'what the dickens'.

entries.clue: Ice mass sheared away a little lower? (4)

blocks.note: a lump of ice that breaks off a glacier or iceberg
a lower is something that lows, like a cow, and a little one is its young

annotation.surface: A glacier sheds a chunk of ice slightly lower down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lower' reads as 'further down' after the ice; said with a cow's 'low' it becomes a mooing animal, and the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A calf is a mass of ice broken off a glacier, and also a small animal that lows, a little lower.

entries.clue: Marriage promise at some other time for admirer (8)

blocks.note: 'I do', the promise at a wedding

annotation.surface: An admirer is offered a proposal that will only be honoured later.
annotation.walkthrough: An idolater is literally an idol-worshipper, so a devoted admirer.
annotation.definitionFit: An extended sense: an idolater worships idols, and loosely anyone who adores a person or thing to excess.

entries.clue: Man following instinctive desires in style (5)

indicatorNotes.following: the first part comes after the second

blocks.note: the id, in Freud, is the part of the mind driven by instinct

annotation.surface: A man follows his instincts in his personal style.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, an island between Britain and Ireland, not a person.
annotation.definitionFit: A less common sense: besides a fixed phrase, idiom is an artist's characteristic manner, as in 'the jazz idiom'.

entries.clue: Group round court extremely elegant (5)

indicatorNotes.extremely: take the extreme letters, the first and last

annotation.surface: A smart group gathers around a court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for elegant; it asks for the word's two ends.
annotation.definitionFit: A general word for a specific one: octets are eight-piece ensembles or sets, one kind of group.

entries.clue: Troops in support for Nelson at Trafalgar? (6)

blocks.note: soldiers marching in a long line
not the 1805 battle but Trafalgar Square in London, where a tall pillar holds up Nelson's statue

annotation.surface: Soldiers backing up Nelson at the Battle of Trafalgar.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface takes you to the sea battle of 1805; the second meaning is Nelson's Column, which holds up his statue in Trafalgar Square, London.
annotation.definitionFit: A column is a line of troops, and Nelson's Column supports his statue in Trafalgar Square.

entries.clue: Small amount for you in Paris sent back (4)

indicatorNotes.sent back: the word goes back the way it came, so it reads backwards

annotation.surface: A small sum meant for you is returned from Paris.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' tells you to use French.
annotation.definitionFit: An iota is a tiny amount, from the smallest Greek letter.

entries.clue: See rook kept by wacky cybernaut (10)

indicatorNotes.kept by: the other letters hold this one inside them
indicatorNotes.wacky: the letters go crazy, into a new order

annotation.surface: Look at a chess rook held by a crazy internet user.
annotation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an instruction to look; it is a noun, a bishop's seat. The R goes among the letters of the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: Canterbury is the see of the Archbishop of Canterbury, head of the Church of England.

entries.clue: Wesleyans denatured alcohol opened by poet (10)

indicatorNotes.opened by: the word is split open and the other placed inside

blocks.note: an odist is a writer of odes

annotation.surface: Teetotal Methodists find their meths broached by a poet.
annotation.walkthrough: Meths is British shorthand for methylated spirits, industrial alcohol made undrinkable. John Wesley founded Methodism.
annotation.definitionFit: Methodists follow John Wesley, so they are Wesleyans.

entries.clue: Characters regularly seen in rougher industrial area (4)

indicatorNotes.Characters regularly seen in: take letters at regular intervals, every other one

blocks.note: the odd-numbered letters of the seven, starting with the first

annotation.surface: Tough characters are found in a rougher manufacturing district.
annotation.walkthrough: The Ruhr is Germany's historic coal and steel region.
annotation.definitionFit: The Ruhr valley is Germany's great industrial area.
